## Where are we in the sorting picture? {.smaller}

| | Best case | Worst case |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| **Insertion** | $O(n)$ | $O(n^2)$ |
| **Selection** | $O(n^2)$ | $O(n^2)$ |
| **Merge** | $O(n\log n)$ | $O(n\log n)$ |

## Complexity of the sorting problem {.smaller}

The ***complexity*** of a problem is the runtime of the ***fastest***
algorithm that solves it.

Today: the complexity of **comparison based sorting**.

- The only thing we can do with two elements is ask $a < b$ — in constant time.
- No peeking inside: no arithmetic, no digits.

\

Insertion, &nbsp; Merge, &nbsp; Quick, &nbsp; Radix, &nbsp; Selection: which are comparison based sorts?

::: notes
Note the shift: not the cost of an *algorithm*, but of the *problem* — the
best any algorithm could ever do.

The list at the bottom: which of these are comparison based? Insertion,
merge, quick and selection all are. **Radix sort is not** — it looks at the
digits of the keys. We haven't seen quick or radix sort; just name them.
:::

## Decision-tree encoding of a sorting algorithm {.smaller}

Suppose you have an unsorted array of length $n$: $p_1\,p_2 \ldots p_n$.
We need to produce a result for every possible arrangement.

Fundamental operation: compare 2 elements using $<$.

::: notes
This is insertion sort on three items, drawn as the comparisons it makes.
Each internal node is a comparison; go left on yes, right on no. Each leaf
is a final order.

**Nothing moves along the way.** In code, the array gets rearranged as the
algorithm runs — a swap here, a shift there. In the tree, the comparisons
only *gather information*: the path you take **encodes** the reordering, and
the leaf announces it all at once. The tree is a record of what the
algorithm learns, not of what it does to the array.

**There's a bug on purpose.** Ask: is every leaf right? To answer, you have
to understand how the tree works. Trace the path $p_1 > p_2$, then
$p_1 < p_3$: that means $p_2 < p_1 < p_3$, so the leaf should be
$p_2\,p_1\,p_3$ — but it says $p_2\,p_3\,p_1$, which also appears at the
far right. One arrangement is missing and another is listed twice.

Once fixed: **6 = 3!** leaves, one for every arrangement. The longest path
has **3 comparisons** — that's the worst-case running time.
:::

## Lower bound on sorting ($n$ items) {.smaller}

Consider a decision tree that arises from a comparison based sorting
algorithm on $n$ items:

- Every permutation must be differentiated by the algorithm.
- There are \_\_\_\_\_\_ permutations.
- Comparisons induce a *binary tree* whose **height** determines the running
  time of the algorithm. (A path is a sequence of comparisons.)
- A binary tree of height $k$ has at most \_\_\_\_ leaves.

We need the shortest tree whose number of leaves is $\ge$ the number of
permutations.

What is the minimum height of a comparison tree for sorting input of size $n$?

::: notes
Blanks: **$n!$** permutations, at most **$2^k$** leaves.

If two different inputs landed on the same leaf, the algorithm would do the
same thing to both and get one of them wrong. So every permutation needs its
own leaf: leaves $\ge n!$.
:::

## Lower bound on sorting ($n$ items) {.smaller}

Find the smallest $k$ so that $2^k \ge n!$

::: notes
Take logs: $k \ge \log(n!)$.

Now bound $\log(n!)$ from below. Half of the factors in
$n! = n(n-1)\cdots 1$ are at least $n/2$, so

$$n! \ge \left(\tfrac{n}{2}\right)^{n/2}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\log(n!) \ge \tfrac{n}{2}\log\tfrac{n}{2} = \Omega(n\log n).$$

And from above, $n! \le n^n$, so $\log(n!) \le n\log n$. So
$\log(n!) = \Theta(n\log n)$.
:::

## Punchline {.smaller}

Lower bound on comparison based sorting ($n$ items)…

\

**Minimum** height of a comparison tree for sorting input of size $n$…

\

\

How tall are the trees for selection and insertion sort?

::: notes
**Any comparison based sort needs $\Omega(n\log n)$ comparisons in the worst
case.** The minimum height is $\lceil\log_2 n!\rceil = \Theta(n\log n)$.

So merge sort is **optimal** among comparison based sorts — asymptotically, you
cannot do better.

Selection and insertion sort: their trees have height $\Theta(n^2)$ —
$n(n-1)/2$ comparisons in the worst case. Selection sort's tree is that tall
on *every* path; insertion sort's has a short path, $n - 1$ comparisons, for
already-sorted input. That's the best case in the table.
:::
